claims.text: The Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi by removing Co.
The initial Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is a fully single-phase solid solution after conventional casting or solidification.
Temperature-dependent dynamic strain aging controls the dynamic mechanical behavior of the Co-free alloy.
Nanoscale short-range-ordered clusters form in the Co-free alloy.
The short-range-ordered clusters are stable and effectively pin dislocations at lower temperatures or high strain rates.
Increasing temperature or decreasing strain rate causes the short-range-ordered clusters to dissolve or become less effective as pinning sites.
Loss of effective short-range-order pinning increases dislocation mobility and ductility while reducing strength.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, Co-free FeNiCrMn will have higher yield and flow stresses at lower temperatures and high strain rates.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, Co-free FeNiCrMn will have greater strain-rate sensitivity at lower temperatures and high strain rates.
The mechanical-response differences between Co-free FeNiCrMn and equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi will diminish as temperature increases or strain rate decreases.
Co in equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi stabilizes homogeneous dislocation motion.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi likely has a more uniform short-range-order state and less pronounced dynamic strain aging than Co-free FeNiCrMn.
The proposed mechanism is applicable only where thermally activated changes in short-range-ordered clusters materially affect dislocation motion.
The controlled comparison spans approximately 77–500 K and strain rates of approximately 10^-4–10^2 s^-1 for both alloys.

Failure to observe a statistically significant low-temperature or high-rate increase in strength and strain-rate sensitivity, or failure to observe correlated temperature-dependent short-range order, is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.
